tasks.q: Which is a reason for testing a program before release?
a: To find and fix errors so it works as intended
To make the code shorter
To add comments to the code
To choose better variable names
tasks.fb: Testing finds bugs before users do. Other reasons: checking it meets the requirements, can't be misused, and has no security weak spots.

tasks.q: Why should testers deliberately try to misuse a program?
a: To check it won't crash or be exploited when users do something unexpected
To make the program run faster
Because users never make mistakes
To find syntax errors only
tasks.fb: Real users type unexpected things and some try to break programs on purpose, so a robust program must cope with both.

tasks.q: When does iterative testing take place?
a: While the program is being developed
Only after the program is released
Once, when the program is finished
Before any code is written
tasks.fb: Iterative testing happens throughout development: each module is tested as it's written.

tasks.q: After fixing a bug in one module, why test the rest of the program again?
a: To check the change hasn't broken code that already worked
Because the bug always moves to another module
To make the program run faster
Testing twice is a rule of Python
tasks.fb: A fix in one place can have side effects elsewhere, so previously working parts are retested.

a: Testing the complete program at the end of development, to check it meets all the requirements
Testing each line as you type it
Testing done by the translator
Testing that happens only if the program crashes
tasks.fb: Final testing happens once the program is complete, before release.

tasks.q: Which is most likely to be checked during final testing?
a: Whether all the modules work together correctly
Whether one loop works just after it's written
Whether a variable name is spelt correctly
Whether the programmer has saved their file
tasks.fb: Iterative testing checks parts as they're built; final testing checks the whole program works together.

a: An error that breaks the rules of the programming language, so the code can't be translated or run
An error that makes the program give the wrong answer
An error caused by the user typing the wrong data
An error in the comments
tasks.fb: Syntax is the grammar of a language. If the translator can't understand a line, the program won't run.

tasks.q: Which line contains a syntax error?
a: prnt("Hello")
total = total + 1
print(total)
if total > 10:
tasks.fb: prnt is a misspelling of the keyword print, so Python doesn't recognise it.

a: The program runs, but doesn't do what the programmer intended
The program won't run at all
The translator reports a mistake
The computer's hardware is faulty
tasks.fb: Logic errors produce wrong results, loop forever or crash at the wrong moment, even though the code follows the rules.

tasks.q: Why are logic errors usually harder to find than syntax errors?
a: The translator doesn't report them, because the code follows the language's rules
They only happen on old computers
They are always hidden in comments
They make the program too fast to see
tasks.fb: You find logic errors by testing and checking the output against what you expected.

tasks.q: Which of these are errors in the total cost program? Select all that apply.
opts: total = total + total should be total = total + 3
Nothing inside the loop reduces items, so it never ends
The input isn't converted to an integer before it is used
return total should be inside the loop
correct: total = total + total should be total = total + 3
Nothing inside the loop reduces items, so it never ends
The input isn't converted to an integer before it is used
tasks.fb: Four errors: the wrong calculation, the missing items = items - 1, the misspelt print, and the missing int().

tasks.q: Which type of error is prnt instead of print?
a: Syntax error
Logic error
Runtime data error
No error
tasks.fb: A misspelt keyword breaks the language's rules, so the code won't run.

tasks.q: Sort each bug: is it a syntax error or a logic error?
items: choice = input(Enter choice:) with no quotation marks
while items >= 1 with the colon missing
valid = True before while not valid:, so the loop never runs
if not choice in [1,2,3]: when input() gives the string "2"
valid == True where valid = True was meant
average = total / count when count is 0
Printing 'Fail' when the score is above the pass mark
tasks.fb: If Python refuses to run the line, it's syntax. If it runs but does the wrong thing, it's logic.

info.title: The first actual bug
info.text: In 1947, engineers working on the Harvard Mark II computer found a moth trapped in a relay. They taped it into their logbook as the 'first actual case of bug being found'.

info.title: Tests that run themselves
info.text: Professional programmers write automated tests that re-run every time the code changes, so iterative testing happens in seconds instead of by hand.

info.title: Alpha and beta testing
info.text: Many games and apps are tested by the developers (alpha testing), then released early to real users (beta testing) to find bugs the developers missed.

info.title: Red squiggly lines
info.text: Most IDEs spot syntax errors as you type and underline them, just like a spell checker. They can't spot logic errors, though.

info.title: A logic error in space
info.text: In 1999, NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter because one team's software used imperial units while another expected metric. The code ran perfectly, but the answer was wrong.

info.title: A very expensive bug
info.text: In 1996, the Ariane 5 rocket self-destructed about 40 seconds after launch. Software reused from the older Ariane 4 tried to store a number too big for its variable.
